section.title: Final Instructions and Greetings
section.sectionRationale: Paul closes the letter with rapid, practical instructions for the life of the church: honor and love those who labor and lead, live at peace, care for the disorderly, the fainthearted, and the weak, never repay evil, and in every circumstance rejoice, pray, and give thanks. He tells them not to quench the Spirit but to test everything and hold the good. Then he grounds it all in a prayer, that the God of peace would Himself sanctify them wholly and keep them blameless until Christ comes, for He who calls them is faithful and will do it.
section.thesis: The shared life of the church is marked by honor for faithful leaders, patient love for one another, and constant joy, prayer, and thanksgiving that keep the Spirit's fire burning; and its confidence rests not on human effort but on the faithful God who calls His people and will Himself sanctify and keep them blameless until the coming of the Lord Jesus.
section.frameNote: Three movements: love and peace within the body, honoring those who lead and bearing with one another; the marks of a Spirit-filled life, rejoicing, praying, giving thanks, and testing all things; and the closing prayer and blessing, that the faithful God who calls will sanctify and keep His people blameless until Christ comes.

units.label: Love and peace within the body
units.note: honor leaders, bear with one another

verses.text: But we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who care for you in the Lord and who {{noutheteo|admonish}} you.
In love, hold them in {{hegeomai|highest regard}} because of their work. Live in peace with one another.
And we urge you, brothers, to admonish the {{ataktos|unruly}}, encourage the {{oligopsychos|fainthearted}}, help the weak, and be patient with everyone.
Make sure that no one repays evil for evil. Always pursue what is good for one another and for all people.

units.label: The marks of a Spirit-filled life
units.note: rejoice, pray, give thanks, test all things

verses.text: {{eucharisteo|Give thanks}} in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.
but {{dokimazo|test}} all things. Hold fast to what is good.
Abstain from every form of evil.

units.label: The faithful God will keep you
units.note: sanctified wholly, kept blameless, by the One who calls

verses.text: Now may the God of peace Himself {{hagiazo|sanctify}} you {{holoteles|completely}}, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept {{amemptos|blameless}} at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The One who {{kaleo|calls}} you is {{pistos|faithful}}, and He will do it.
Brothers, pray for us as well.
Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss.
I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers.
The {{charis|grace}} of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

noutheteo.gloss: To admonish, warn, or counsel by putting truth into someone's mind. It describes the loving correction that leaders give and that the whole church is to give the unruly. Far from harshness, it is the caring instruction of those who watch over souls and want to see one another kept from harm.

hegeomai.gloss: To consider, esteem, or hold in regard. Paul tells the church to hold their leaders in the highest regard in love, because of their work. The esteem is not for status but for faithful labor, and it is bound together with love, so that respect for leaders and warmth toward them go hand in hand.

ataktos.gloss: Disorderly, unruly, out of rank, a military term for a soldier who breaks step. It describes those in the church living undisciplined or idle lives, out of line with the gospel. They are to be admonished, corrected in love, not abandoned, so that they may return to ordered, faithful living.

oligopsychos.gloss: Fainthearted, small-souled, discouraged. It pictures those whose spirits have grown faint under pressure or fear. Rather than being pushed, they are to be encouraged, come alongside and strengthened, so that the weary and downcast are lifted rather than left behind.

chairo.gloss: To rejoice, to be glad. Paul commands joy at all times, a settled gladness in God that does not depend on circumstances. This joy is not forced cheerfulness but the fruit of belonging to the Lord, possible even in affliction because its source is Christ and not changing conditions.

adialeiptos.gloss: Without ceasing, constantly, without interruption. Prayer is to be unceasing, not meaning endless words but a continual, God-ward turning of the heart that runs through all of life. It describes a life kept in constant communion with God rather than prayer confined to set moments.

eucharisteo.gloss: To give thanks, to be grateful. Believers are to give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God's will for them in Christ Jesus. Thanksgiving is not for every circumstance as though all were good, but in every circumstance, trusting the God who works all things for the good of His people.

sbennymi.gloss: To quench or extinguish, as one puts out a fire. The Spirit's work is pictured as flame, and the church is warned not to smother it. To quench the Spirit is to resist or stifle His work, whether by despising His gifts or by choking off the life He gives; instead His fire is to be kept burning.

propheteia.gloss: Prophecy, a Spirit-prompted word for the building up of the church. Paul warns against treating such words with contempt, yet in the same breath calls for testing. Prophecy is neither to be despised nor swallowed uncritically; it is to be weighed against the truth and received only where it proves good.

dokimazo.gloss: To test, examine, and prove, as metal is tested for genuineness. Believers are to test all things, weighing every claim and teaching, then holding fast to what is good and rejecting what is evil. Discernment, not gullibility and not cynicism, is the mark of a Spirit-filled and mature church.

hagiazo.gloss: To sanctify, to make holy, to set apart wholly for God. Paul prays that the God of peace Himself would sanctify the believers. Holiness is here God's own work in His people, and the prayer looks for it to be complete, reaching the whole person and bringing them to the day of Christ set apart for Him.

holoteles.gloss: Wholly, completely, through and through, reaching every part to the very end. Paul prays that God would sanctify them completely, and then that their entire spirit, soul, and body be kept. The word stresses that God's sanctifying work leaves nothing out; it claims the whole person for holiness.

amemptos.gloss: Blamelessly, without fault or reproach. The prayer is that the whole person would be kept blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus. This is not sinless perfection achieved now but the settled goal of God's keeping, a people preserved and made ready to stand unashamed before Christ on that day.

kaleo.gloss: To call, to summon effectively into fellowship with God. The One who calls is God, whose call is not a mere invitation but a powerful summons that creates what it commands. Because the calling is God's own work, the security of the believer rests on His faithfulness to complete what He has begun.

pistos.gloss: Faithful, trustworthy, reliable. The One who calls His people is faithful, and He will do it. The whole weight of the closing prayer rests here: sanctification and preservation are certain not because believers are strong but because God is faithful to His promise and will surely bring His work to completion.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's unearned favor and kindness in Christ. Paul ends as he began, with grace, praying that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ would be with them. The letter opens and closes in grace, framing every command and every hope within the free favor of God given through His Son.

basic.context: Paul brings the letter to a close with a burst of short, practical commands for church life. He asks them to honor and love the leaders who work hard among them, to live in peace, and to care for the different needs of the disorderly, the fainthearted, and the weak, never repaying evil but always pursuing good. Then come the well-known calls to rejoice always, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything, along with the warning not to quench the Spirit but to test all things and hold the good. He seals it with a prayer: that the God of peace would sanctify them completely and keep them blameless until Christ comes, because the God who calls them is faithful and will do it.
basic.hermeneutics: These are commands for ordinary Christian life together, not a random list but the shape of a healthy church. Yet Paul does not leave them as bare duties. He ends by praying that God Himself would accomplish this holiness, and he grounds the whole thing in God's faithfulness. So the passage teaches how believers are to live while resting on the God who works that life in them.
basic.originalLanguages: The church is to noutheteo, admonish, the ataktos, unruly, encourage the oligopsychos, fainthearted, and hold leaders in hegeomai, high regard. They are to chairo, rejoice, always, pray adialeiptos, without ceasing, and eucharisteo, give thanks, in everything. They must not sbennymi, quench, the Spirit or despise propheteia, prophecy, but dokimazo, test, all things. Paul prays that God would hagiazo, sanctify, them holoteles, completely, and keep them amemptos, blameless, for the One who kaleo, calls, them is pistos, faithful. He ends with charis, grace.
basic.typology: The prayer that God would sanctify and keep His people takes up the Old Testament longing for a holy people fit to dwell with a holy God, now answered as God Himself makes them holy in Christ. The unquenched Spirit recalls the fire that was never to go out on the altar, kept burning as a sign of God's abiding presence among His people.
basic.christ: Every command here is life in Christ Jesus, and the whole passage is bracketed by His grace. It is at His coming that the church will be found blameless, and it is His grace with which the letter ends. The holiness Paul prays for is not self-made but the gift of the God of peace, secured by the faithful One who calls, and it is aimed at the day when believers will stand unashamed before the Lord Jesus.
basic.god: God is the God of peace who sanctifies His people, and He is the faithful One who calls them and will surely complete His work. The confidence of the passage rests on His character: He does not merely command holiness, He accomplishes it. Because the God who calls is faithful, the believer's final blamelessness is as certain as God's own reliability.
basic.crossReferences: Philippians 4 also calls believers to rejoice always and to pray with thanksgiving. Philippians 1 promises that He who began a good work will bring it to completion. And Hebrews 13 speaks of the God of peace equipping His people to do His will through Jesus.
basic.oneStory: God has always been working toward a holy people who can dwell with Him. Here at the letter's close, Paul prays that the God of peace would finish that work, sanctifying His people completely and keeping them blameless until Christ appears. The commands describe the life of that people now, and the promise assures them that the faithful God who called them will carry them all the way to the day of the Lord.

context.literary:
The closing of a Pauline letter normally moves from exhortation to a prayer wish to greetings and a blessing, and this one follows the pattern while compressing a great deal into a short space. Verses 12 to 22 are a run of brief imperatives, many only two or three words long in Greek, and the pace itself teaches something. In the BSB the commands come almost like a drumbeat: acknowledge, hold in highest regard, live in peace, admonish, encourage, help, be patient, make sure, pursue, rejoice, pray, give thanks, do not extinguish, do not treat with contempt, test, hold fast, abstain.

The list has a rough order. Verses 12 and 13 concern relations between the church and those who lead it. Verses 14 and 15 widen to relations among all the members and with outsiders, using three different verbs for three different needs and ending with 'all people.' Verses 16 to 18 step back from the community to the believer's posture before God, three short sentences that have been memorized by generations of Christians. Verses 19 to 22 take up the church's life with the Spirit and with prophecy. The pairing of prohibitions and positive commands in 19 to 21 forms a compact run of linked commands: do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies, test everything, hold fast the good, and abstain from evil.

Then the register changes. At verse 23 the commands stop and a prayer begins, introduced by a strong 'Now may the God of peace Himself.' The pronoun 'Himself,' autos, is emphatic and stands against the long list of things the church is told to do. What they have been asked to attempt, God will accomplish. Verse 24 gives the reason in one short sentence: 'The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it.' The remaining verses, a request for prayer, a greeting, a solemn charge to read the letter aloud, and the blessing, are the ordinary frame of an apostolic letter, and yet they have the same shape as the whole: people asking one another for help, and grace over all.
context.historical:
The 'brothers' of this closing are a house church in a Greek commercial city, small enough that Paul can speak of all of them as a family, and recently formed enough that its leadership was still taking shape. The people he describes, those who 'work diligently,' 'preside over you in the Lord' and 'give you instruction,' are not yet described by office titles. Paul does not say bishops or elders here, and the three phrases are governed by one article in Greek, which suggests one group seen from three sides. It is likely that these were the older or more settled members who had taken on the burden of caring for the others, possibly including the host of the gatherings, a patron in whose home they met. Their authority was real but modest, and it rested on their labor.

The church had come under strain. Chapters 2 and 3 describe persecution. Chapter 4 corrects confusions about sexual conduct and work. The three categories of verse 14 correspond well to what has been seen so far in the letter: some members were apparently idle or disorderly, which Paul addresses again in 2 Thessalonians 3:6 to 15; some were anxious about the dead and the Day, chapters 4 and 5; and some were weak, which could mean weak in faith, in conscience or in resources. A Greek city also had its own standards of honor and vengeance, in which repaying injury with injury was seen as prudent. Verse 15 sets the church against that.

The mention of prophecy shows that spiritual gifts were active in the church. Prophetic speech in the ancient world was not unusual, since pagan oracles abounded, and it was necessary to test who was speaking and by whose power. Prophets in the Corinthian church had to be weighed, 1 Corinthians 14:29, and in the early Christian communities the false and the true both appeared.

The holy kiss was an ordinary sign of family greeting in the Mediterranean world that Christians took over to mark the family of God, as Romans 16:16, 1 Corinthians 16:20 and 2 Corinthians 13:12 show. The charge to have the letter read aloud to all matters because most people could not read it themselves, and because a letter delivered to a few leaders could be kept from the rest. Reading aloud was how the congregation heard the apostle.
context.canonical:
Several of the commands here repeat an Old Testament pattern. To rejoice, give thanks and pray are the three continuous postures of the Psalter. 'Hold fast to what is good' and 'abstain from evil' recall the repeated choice set before Israel, Amos 5:14 and 15 and Psalm 34:14. The instruction about not repaying evil for evil is Proverbs 20:22 and 24:29 in the mouth of an apostle, and Paul will repeat it in Romans 12:17 to 19, adding that vengeance belongs to God.

The New Testament parallels are close. Philippians 4:4 to 7, 'Rejoice in the Lord always... in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God,' shows that the triad here is Paul's regular pattern of life. The summary of what believers owe each other in Romans 12:9 to 18 covers much of the same ground, with the same call to peace. Hebrews 13:17 gives the same teaching about leaders, who watch over souls as those who must give an account.

The prayer of verse 23 has a close cousin in Hebrews 13:20 and 21, where the God of peace equips the church with every good thing to do His will. The promise of 1 Corinthians 1:8 and 9 is almost a doublet of verse 24: God will sustain you to the end, blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, and He is faithful, having called you into fellowship with His Son. Jude 24 gives the same assurance in the form of a doxology, to the One who is able to keep you from stumbling and present you unblemished in His glorious presence with great joy. Philippians 1:6 says that He who began a good work will carry it on to completion.

The commands about the Spirit and prophecy have Old Testament roots as well. Moses longed that all the LORD's people were prophets and that He would put His Spirit on them, Numbers 11:29, and Joel 2:28 promised that the Spirit would be poured out on all flesh. At Pentecost Peter says the promise has come, Acts 2:17 and 18. Paul's instruction to test and hold fast is the discipline of a church living in that outpouring.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul closes by showing the church how its shared life works when it is working. The commands are not random. They begin with the people closest to the center of the church, its leaders, and move outward, and what ties them together is love expressed as attention to what each person needs. The verbs in verse 14 are chosen for different conditions: the unruly need to be warned, the fainthearted to be steadied, the weak to be held on to. A single response to all three would fail at least two of them.

He also means to give the church a pattern for its inner life with God. The three brief commands of verses 16 to 18 are put in the plainest language, because they are meant to be carried into every circumstance. 'This is God's will for you in Christ Jesus' tells the church that these are not optional embellishments to a serious faith but the center of what God wants from it. They are also not heroic; they describe a way of being present before God that any believer can begin today.

He wants the Spirit's work welcomed and examined. Many churches err by treating all spiritual speech as automatically right, or by treating all of it as suspect. Paul avoids both. He calls for openness and for testing in the same breath.

Above all, he intends the prayer to carry the weight. He has just given eleven or so commands, and then he says that God Himself will sanctify them and keep them. He does not want the commands to be heard as a burden that rests on the church alone. They are the shape of a life that God is already producing, and verse 24 gives the church something to lean on when it finds the commands beyond it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is among the most prescriptive passages in the letter. Nearly every verse from 12 to 22 is a command, and they are addressed to the whole church, not only to leaders. There is little here to treat as description. The instructions can be received as given, with attention to the situation and the condition they have in view.

That said, application needs some care. The command to greet with a holy kiss is a prescription of the substance, a warm and visible welcome to fellow believers, in the form that the culture of the time used, and churches throughout history have kept the substance while using handshakes, embraces or other fitting customs. The command to 'rejoice at all times' is not a command to feel cheerful in grief; Paul himself speaks of sorrow in other places, and the verse is best read as a call to the settled joy that exists alongside sorrow, as 2 Corinthians 6:10 says, 'sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.' To 'pray without ceasing' is not a call to be on one's knees all day but to keep up a steady habit of turning to God. And 'give thanks in every circumstance' is not 'give thanks for every circumstance'; it does not ask the bereaved to be thankful for the death but to be thankful in the midst of it.

The prayer and promise of verses 23 and 24 are descriptive of what God will do, and they are not commands. The right response is trust, not effort.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by 'spirit, soul, and body' in verse 23?

views.label: Three distinct parts (trichotomy)
views.case: Verse 23 lists spirit, soul and body, and Hebrews 4:12 speaks of the word of God dividing soul and spirit. On this view human beings have a material body, an animating soul, and a spirit that communes with God, and sanctification touches all three.

views.label: Two parts, with different names for the immaterial side (dichotomy)
views.case: Scripture often uses soul and spirit interchangeably, as in Mary's song, Luke 1:46 and 47, and treats death as the separation of body and spirit or soul. Paul piles up terms for emphasis here, as Jesus does when He lists heart, soul, mind and strength in Mark 12:30. The list means the whole person, and is not an anatomy.

views.label: Aspects of one whole person (holistic)
views.case: Many recent scholars hold that Paul is not offering an analysis of human parts at all. The word 'entire,' holokleron, stresses completeness, and the phrase is a rhetorical flourish pointing to every dimension of life being included in God's keeping.

debates.bearing: The point of the verse is not the number of parts but the extent of the promise. God's sanctifying work reaches the whole person, and no part of a believer's life lies beyond His care. Believers can hold any of the three views and keep the meaning.

debates.question: How should the church treat prophecy, and does it continue today?

views.label: Prophecy continues, and is to be tested
views.case: This view holds that the gift Paul describes remains active, usually as Spirit-prompted speech that is fallible and must be weighed, as 1 Corinthians 14:29 requires. The command to test everything shows that prophecy is not the same as Scripture, and so it can be welcomed without being treated as having the authority of the apostles.

views.label: Prophecy ceased with the apostolic age
views.case: Cessationists argue that the gifts of revelation served to establish the church and the New Testament, and that with the completion of Scripture such gifts ended. They read verses 19 to 21 as instructions for the first generation, and in later times apply the principle of testing to every claim to speak for God.

views.label: The command is about any word claiming God's voice
views.case: A third reading puts less weight on the gift question and more on the principle. Whether or not the gift continues, 1 John 4:1 shows that believers must always 'test the spirits,' and verse 21's twin commands, test everything and hold fast to what is good, apply to every sermon, book and claim of guidance.

debates.bearing: Both camps agree on what the verse most plainly requires: do not despise what may be from the Spirit and do not swallow it whole. Openness without testing makes a church gullible, and testing without openness makes it cold.

debates.question: What is 'every form of evil' in verse 22?

views.label: Every kind of evil
views.case: The Greek eidos can mean a kind or sort, and this reading, followed by the BSB, takes the command as a call to avoid evil in every variety.

views.label: Every appearance of evil
views.case: Eidos can also mean outward appearance, as in 2 Corinthians 5:7, 'not by sight.' Older English versions took it so, and the command then warns against conduct that looks evil to others, in line with Paul's concern elsewhere that believers avoid giving needless offense.

views.label: Every kind of evil that presents itself as good
views.case: Set against the preceding command to test everything, the phrase can be taken as 'whatever form evil takes,' including the disguised forms that need testing to unmask. This keeps the sense of kind while explaining why the command follows the call to test.

debates.bearing: The surrounding commands to test and hold fast give the verse its function. Believers are to examine what comes before them and reject what is bad however it is dressed.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 12 describes three activities of the leaders in a single phrase. The first, kopiontas, 'work diligently,' is from kopos, toil to the point of weariness, the same noun Paul used of his own labor in 2:9 and of the Thessalonians' 'labor of love' in 1:3. The second, proistamenoi, 'preside over,' literally means to stand before, and can mean either to lead or to care for. Paul uses the same verb of a household manager in 1 Timothy 3:4 and of the one who leads in Romans 12:8. The sense of caring is probably present, so that leadership here is closer to oversight with concern than to rule. The third, noutheteo in the participle, 'give instruction,' literally means to put in mind, to admonish, and shows that part of a leader's work is correction offered in love. The same verb appears in verse 14 for the duty of all the members to 'admonish the unruly,' so the responsibility is shared.

Verse 14 has three distinct needs. The word for 'unruly,' ataktoi, belongs to the military vocabulary of rank and order: soldiers out of formation. The cognate adverb appears in 2 Thessalonians 3:6 and 11 for those who live in an undisciplined way, and in Paul's usage the word points to idleness. 'Fainthearted' translates oligopsychoi, literally small-souled, people whose courage has shrunk, probably under persecution or grief. The 'weak,' asthenoi, are to be 'helped,' antechomai, a verb that means to hold on to, to cling to, as in Titus 1:9 where the elder holds firmly to the trustworthy word. The church is to take hold of the weak and not let them slip. 'Be patient' translates makrothymeo, literally long-tempered. It is the Greek counterpart of the Old Testament description of God as slow to anger, Exodus 34:6, and it appears among the qualities of love in 1 Corinthians 13:4.

The command of verse 17, adialeiptos, 'without ceasing,' is an adverb describing something that is not interrupted, in the way a cough or a recurring fever is never absent, though it may subside. Paul uses it of his own continual prayer for the Thessalonians in 1:2 and 2:13 and of his prayer for the Romans in Romans 1:9. It describes a habit of constant return, not unbroken speech.

In verse 19, 'do not extinguish,' sbennymi, means to put out a fire or a lamp. Jesus uses it for the smoldering wick He will not snuff out, Matthew 12:20, and the foolish virgins say their lamps are going out, Matthew 25:8. The Spirit is spoken of as a flame that can be damped down by contempt, and 'test,' dokimazo, in verse 21, is the verb for assaying metal. Paul uses it for the fire that tests each person's work in 1 Corinthians 3:13 and for the discernment of what is God's will in Romans 12:2.

Verse 23 prays for sanctification 'completely,' and for the 'entire' person, holokleron, a word whose sense is wholeness, every part present and none missing. It appears in James 1:4, where perseverance is to make believers 'complete, lacking nothing.' Verse 27 begins 'I charge you,' enorkizo, a verb built on horkos, oath, which puts the readers under solemn obligation before the Lord to see the letter read to all.

typology.type: The fire on the altar, Leviticus 6:12 and 13
typology.fulfillment: The priests were to keep the fire on the altar burning continually, adding wood each morning, and 'it must not be extinguished,' Leviticus 6:13. The word of the command is the same one that Paul uses of the Spirit in verse 19, to quench or put out. The altar fire was the sign that the way to God stayed open and that sacrifice could be offered at any hour. In Christ the fire is no longer confined to a courtyard altar but burns in the church. At Pentecost the Spirit came as tongues of fire resting on each believer, Acts 2:3, and Paul tells Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God, 2 Timothy 1:6. The type is limited, because the priests kept the flame by feeding it wood, while the Spirit is given by God and is kept by welcome and not by fuel.

typology.type: The consecration of priests, Exodus 29 and Leviticus 20:8
typology.fulfillment: Israel's priests could not make themselves holy. The LORD said He would consecrate Aaron and his sons, Exodus 29:44, and told all Israel, 'I am the LORD who sanctifies you,' Leviticus 20:8. Paul's prayer that the God of peace Himself would sanctify the church completely is that same truth carried over to a whole people. Peter calls the church a royal priesthood and a holy nation, 1 Peter 2:9. The escalation in Christ is that sanctification no longer requires washing in a basin and garments of cloth, but a washing by His blood and the Spirit's work in the heart, Hebrews 10:10 and 14. The old consecration was repeated; the new is complete for all who are in Him.

typology.type: The Spirit on all the LORD's people, Numbers 11:25 to 29
typology.fulfillment: When the Spirit rested on the seventy elders and they prophesied, Joshua asked Moses to stop two men who were prophesying in the camp. Moses replied, 'I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!' Numbers 11:29. Paul's command not to treat prophecies with contempt belongs to the age in which Moses' wish is being fulfilled. Joel foretold it, Joel 2:28, and Peter proclaims it at Pentecost, Acts 2:17 and 18. The correspondence is that a gift once given to a few for a season is now given to a whole people. The earlier scene shows too the need for discernment, since Joshua was zealous in the wrong direction, and Paul's testing guards against both contempt and credulity.

typology.type: The public reading of the law, Deuteronomy 31:11 to 13 and Nehemiah 8:3
typology.fulfillment: Moses commanded that the law be read in the hearing of all Israel, men, women, children and foreigners, so that all might listen and learn to fear the LORD, Deuteronomy 31:11 and 12. Ezra read it aloud from daybreak until noon to everyone who could understand, Nehemiah 8:3. Paul's solemn charge that the letter be read to all the brothers puts an apostolic letter in the same place: it is to be heard by the whole assembly, not kept by a few. The line is deliberate, since Paul treats his words as carrying the Lord's authority, as 2:13 says. The pattern continues in Colossians 4:16 and in the later public reading of the Scriptures in the church. The type falls short in that the older reading had to be repeated at set times, while the church's reading is the regular rhythm of its weekly life.

study.christ:
Christ stands in this passage not as a topic but as the setting of everything. Three small phrases carry him: 'in Christ Jesus' in verse 18, 'at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ' in verse 23, and 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ' in verse 28. The commands are bracketed by his presence, and each bracket says something different.

The first phrase, 'this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus,' tells us that joy, prayer and thanksgiving are possible only in union with him. Outside Christ, rejoicing always would be self-deception and unceasing prayer a habit with no listener. In Christ it is the natural condition of a person who has been reconciled to the Father. Jesus Himself prayed to His Father with thanks before great trials, as at the tomb of Lazarus, John 11:41, and at the table before His death, Luke 22:17 and 19. The Christian life of rejoicing, praying and thanking is the life of Jesus shared with those who belong to Him.

The second phrase looks forward. The blamelessness for which Paul prays is to be seen 'at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.' He is the Judge before whom believers will stand, and also the one who makes them able to stand. 1 John 2:28 tells believers to remain in Him so that at His appearing they may be confident and unashamed. Jude 24 speaks of His ability to present them unblemished in His glorious presence with great joy. The same Lord who comes in glory comes for the sake of a people He has already cleansed.

The third phrase, the closing grace, makes every command a response to a gift. The Lord Jesus Christ is the source of the grace that sanctifies. The God of peace of verse 23 is the God who, as Hebrews 13:20 says, brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, and 'through the blood of the eternal covenant' makes His people complete. Peace with God, which verse 23 names, was won on the cross, Romans 5:1, and Christ Himself is called 'our peace' in Ephesians 2:14.

Christ is also the pattern for the community life of verses 12 to 15. He was the one who worked for His people, who bore with the weak, who refused to repay evil for evil, 1 Peter 2:23, and who sought the good of all, even His enemies. The call to patience with everyone has its model in the patience of the Lord, 2 Peter 3:9. Yet we should avoid laying a Christological meaning on every command. Some of the commands are simply wise and holy counsel. What the passage requires is that they be done in His name and by His grace, and that the believer look past them to the One who is faithful.

The Spirit whom believers are not to quench is the Spirit of Christ, Romans 8:9, and the prophetic word to be weighed is a word that must agree with the testimony of Jesus, Revelation 19:10.
study.god:
The passage names God three ways, and each tells us something. He is the God of peace, he is the one who calls, and he is the faithful one who will do what he has called us to. The commands of verses 12 to 22 are surrounded by a theology that guarantees their fulfilment.

The title 'the God of peace' is a favorite of Paul's, found in Romans 15:33, 16:20, Philippians 4:9 and Hebrews 13:20. Peace here is not just the absence of conflict but wholeness, the shalom of the Old Testament, in which everything is in right order. The title is placed beside the instruction to 'live in peace with one another' in verse 13, and it names the source: the church's peace is a reflection of its God. A congregation torn by rivalry is out of step with the character of the one it worships. Yet the same God is the one who, in the Old Testament, brings both peace and judgment, and the peace of this title has been made at the cost of the cross.

The verb 'sanctify' says that holiness is God's own work. Leviticus 20:8 says 'I am the LORD who sanctifies you.' The pronoun 'Himself' in verse 23 insists that the church's holiness is not self-produced. This is not a license for passivity, since the commands stand, but it places the work where it belongs. The fuller reach of the promise, spirit, soul and body, shows that no part of a person is outside the territory God intends to claim.

The call of verse 24 is the heart of the doctrine of God here. God is the one who calls, in the present tense of continuing character. He called the Thessalonians through the gospel, 2 Thessalonians 2:14, and to His own kingdom and glory, 1 Thessalonians 2:12. Because He is the one who called, the completion of the work depends on Him and not on the quality of their response. The grounding term is 'faithful,' pistos, which in the Old Testament is the character of the God who keeps covenant, Deuteronomy 7:9. He does not abandon what He starts, as Philippians 1:6 says, and His faithfulness is not diminished by the weakness of those He calls, 2 Timothy 2:13.

Finally, there is the God who works through human beings. He appoints leaders who labor, He asks the church to admonish and encourage and help, and He commands prayer for the apostles, verse 25. He does not bypass these means. Yet He also reminds the church that the means are His to use, not the other way around. For worship the passage yields a rhythm: the congregation hears the commands, asks for strength, and receives the promise with a confident amen. The tension is that God commands what He alone can give, and the Bible never sees that as a contradiction. Augustine's old prayer, give what You command and command what You will, captures it.

crossReferences.note: Rejoice always, let your gentleness be known, bring requests to God with thanksgiving, and the peace of God will guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. It is the same triad of joy, prayer and thanks as verses 16 to 18, with the promise of peace that verse 23 also holds out.

Do not repay anyone evil for evil, live at peace with everyone, and leave room for God's wrath. This extends 1 Thessalonians 5:15 by giving the reason: vengeance belongs to the Lord, which frees believers to pursue good.

The prophets should speak in turn and the others weigh what is said, for the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. It gives practical content to 'test all things' and shows how the Thessalonian instruction worked in another congregation.

Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. It uses the same verb as 'test' in 1 Thessalonians 5:21 and gives the reason: many false prophets have gone out into the world.

God will sustain you to the end so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, and God is faithful. It is a near twin of verses 23 and 24, written from the same period, showing that blamelessness and God's faithfulness were a settled pair in Paul's thought.

The God of peace who brought back Jesus from the dead equips believers with every good thing to do His will and works in them what pleases Him. It repeats the structure of the passage, a title of God, a prayer for His work in the church, and a doxology to Christ.

A doxology to the One who is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them unblemished before His glory with great joy. It answers the prayer of verse 23 in the form of praise, and it shows that the keeping of verse 24 is a matter for confident worship.

The altar fire must be kept burning and not extinguished. The command is the Old Testament picture behind 'do not extinguish the Spirit,' and it shows what Paul's readers might have heard when he used the word for putting out a fire.

Moses wishes that all the LORD's people were prophets with the Spirit upon them. The wish lies behind the command not to despise prophecy, since a church in which the Spirit speaks is the fruit of that wish.

Believers are to obey their leaders, who watch over their souls as those who must give an account, so that they may do it with joy. It matches 1 Thessalonians 5:12 and 13 in treating leaders as burdened workers whom the church should make glad.

Paul returns to the unruly with fuller instruction, telling the church to keep away from those who live undisciplined lives and yet not to treat them as enemies. It shows what 'admonish the unruly' came to mean in practice at Thessalonica.

He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. This is the promise of verse 24 stated in another letter, resting on the same ground: the one who starts the work is the one who finishes it.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is the story of a God who wants a people He can live among, and of how the people He made in His image became unfit for His presence. The law at Sinai tried to describe holiness in detail. The prophets longed for a day when God would write His law on hearts and give His Spirit so that His people would walk in His ways, Ezekiel 36:26 and 27. This passage is a small portrait of that day arrived. A church of ordinary people, in a commercial port, is living out peace, patience, prayer and thanksgiving, with leaders who work and a Spirit who speaks.

It answers a question the story had left open: how can a holy God dwell with a people who are not holy? The answer here is that He sanctifies them Himself. The earlier answer, in the tabernacle, was ritual and distance, with a veil and a priest. Now the sanctifying is done by the God of peace, through the death of Christ, by the Spirit who dwells in the church, and the church is told not to put out His fire.

It also sets up what follows. The commands describe the people of God in the interval between the first and second comings, living as the community of the new age within the old. The prayer looks to 'the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ' as the day on which the work will be finished. The letter's three themes, the church's faith and love, its hope in Christ's coming, and its holiness, come together here in a single sentence. The pattern recurs in other letters: Paul ends a letter by praying that God would finish what He has begun, as in 1 Corinthians 1:8 and 9 and Philippians 1:6.

The end of the story is anticipated in the word 'blameless.' In the final chapters of Scripture the people of God stand before His throne, washed and unashamed, Revelation 7:14 and 15, and Revelation 21:3 says He will dwell with them. The commands here, to honor the faithful, to bear with the weak, to refuse revenge, and to pray without ceasing, are the training for a people who will live in a world where all those things are simply natural. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, with which the letter ends, is both the first thing that was given to the church and the last thing it will need, since it is by grace that the God who calls will bring His people home.

sermon.title: All the Called Are Kept: 1 Thessalonians 5:23-28, Part 3
sermon.why: Piper works through the closing prayer to show that the sanctifying and keeping of believers rests on God's faithfulness, unfolding verse 24, He who calls you is faithful and He will do it, as the ground of the church's assurance.

quiz.q: How does Paul say the church should treat those who labor and lead among them?

options.text: Acknowledge them and hold them in the highest regard in love, because of their work.
options.note: Verses 12 and 13 call for esteem and love toward faithful leaders.

options.text: Obey them without ever weighing what they teach.
options.note: Respect is due, but Paul also calls the church to test all things.

options.text: Treat them the same as everyone else, with no special regard.
options.note: Paul urges special esteem for them because of their labor.

options.text: Suspect them and keep them at a distance.
options.note: The command is love and high regard, not suspicion.

quiz.q: What three brief commands does Paul give for a Spirit-filled life in verses 16 to 18?

options.text: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in every circumstance.
options.note: Verses 16 to 18 give exactly these three, calling it God's will in Christ.

options.text: Rejoice only when things go well, and pray occasionally.
options.note: Paul commands constant joy and unceasing prayer, not occasional.

options.text: Work hard, stay quiet, and avoid other people.
options.note: These are not the commands; the marks are joy, prayer, and thanks.

options.text: Give thanks only for the good things that happen.
options.note: It is thanks in every circumstance, trusting God through all of them.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by not quenching the Spirit?

options.text: Do not stifle the Spirit's work; instead test everything and hold fast to what is good.
options.note: Verses 19 to 21 pair not quenching the Spirit with testing and holding the good.

options.text: Accept every claimed word from anyone without question.
options.note: Paul honors the Spirit but commands testing, not uncritical acceptance.

options.text: Ignore prophecy and spiritual gifts entirely.
options.note: That would quench the Spirit; Paul says do not treat prophecies with contempt.

options.text: Suppress all emotion in worship.
options.note: The concern is the Spirit's work, not the presence or absence of emotion.

quiz.q: What does Paul pray for the church in verse 23?

options.text: That the God of peace would sanctify them completely and keep them blameless until Christ comes.
options.note: Verse 23 is a prayer for complete sanctification and preservation.

options.text: That they would make themselves perfect by their own effort.
options.note: It is God who sanctifies; the holiness is His work in them.

options.text: That they would be spared all hardship in this life.
options.note: The prayer is for holiness and preservation, not a life free of trouble.

options.text: That only their souls, not their bodies, would be saved.
options.note: Paul prays for the whole person, spirit, soul, and body.

quiz.q: On what does Paul rest the certainty that God will sanctify and keep His people?

options.text: On God's faithfulness: the One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it.
options.note: Verse 24 grounds the assurance in God's faithfulness, not human strength.

options.text: On the believers' success at keeping all the commands.
options.note: The commands matter, but the certainty rests on God, who will do it.

options.text: On the leaders being strong enough to hold the church together.
options.note: The confidence is in the faithful God, not in human leaders.

options.text: On the hope that God might change His mind and help.
options.note: God is faithful and will surely do it; it is not a hope He might act.

questions: Paul asks the church to honor and love those who labor among them. Who has worked hard for your soul, and how could you show them real regard this week?
Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. Which of these three do you find hardest right now, and why?

Paul warns against quenching the Spirit while also urging us to test all things. Where do you lean, toward stifling the Spirit or toward accepting things uncritically, and how might you grow in discerning openness?

Paul prays that God would sanctify you completely, spirit, soul, and body. What part of your life still feels far from that whole-person holiness, and how does it help to know God Himself does this work?
He who calls you is faithful, and He will do it. How does resting on God's faithfulness, rather than your own effort, change the way you pursue holiness?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered unruly is a military term for one out of rank or breaking step, describing the idle and disorderly rather than merely the rebellious.
The BSB footnote offers an alternative rendering, may your spirit, soul, and body be kept entirely blameless, keeping the sense of the whole person preserved for the day of Christ.
The BSB footnote observes that the Byzantine and Textus Receptus traditions add Amen at the end of the letter.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 1 Thessalonians 5:12-28. All seventeen verses confirmed; none required correction. Footnotes at 5:23 and 5:28 recorded in translationNotes.
